## TAAFT - There's An AI For That

### Key Highlights
- Meta is reportedly building an AI version of its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, trained on his mannerisms, tone, and internal strategy thinking.
- Claude, an AI tool, now integrates with Microsoft Word to provide AI contract review, redlining, and clause editing.
- The first data center in space is live, operated by Kepler Communications, featuring 40 NVIDIA Orin GPUs across 10 satellites linked by laser.
- Google has launched a free AI skills hub, offering beginner courses and hands-on labs for Gemini, Vertex AI, and prompt engineering.
- Stanford has published a full lesson on AI agents, covering topics such as prompt chaining, RAG pipelines, and agent anatomy.

### Detailed Points
- The TAAFT newsletter covers various AI developments, including Meta's AI version of Mark Zuckerberg, which aims to allow employees to interact with a digital version of the CEO when he is unavailable.
- Claude's integration with Microsoft Word enables legal contract review, redlining, and clause editing directly inside Word, with native tracked changes.
- The data center in space, operated by Kepler Communications, has the potential for numerous applications, including remote OS boot across multiple spacecraft.
- Google's AI skills hub provides a comprehensive resource for individuals to learn about AI, with courses and labs on Gemini, Vertex AI, and prompt engineering.
- Stanford's lesson on AI agents dives into the details of building and working with AI agents, including prompt chaining and RAG pipelines.
- Other AI tools and developments mentioned include Lindy, Bluor, TranslaBuddy, Hal9, and more, each offering unique capabilities such as calendar management, marketing email generation, and translation services.
- The newsletter also mentions the AI Tools Starter Pack, a collection of 99 prompts tested and refined by the TAAFT team, designed to work with various AI models like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

## Uncovering AI

### Key Highlights
- Stanford released its annual AI report card, the AI Index 2026, highlighting significant growth in AI adoption and capability.
- Google launched Lyria 3 Pro, a music generation model that can create full-length songs, marking a significant advancement in AI-powered music production.
- A PwC study found that 20% of companies are capturing 74% of AI's economic value, indicating a widening gap between AI leaders and laggards.

### Detailed Points
- The Stanford AI Index 2026 reported that generative AI has reached 53% population adoption within three years, faster than the personal computer or the internet.
- The estimated value of generative AI tools to U.S. consumers has already reached $172 billion annually by early 2026, with the median value per user tripling between 2025 and 2026.
- The most powerful AI models are also the least transparent, with the Foundation Model Transparency Index dropping from 58 to 40 points this year.
- Google's Lyria 3 Pro music generation model can create tracks up to three minutes long, a six-fold increase from its predecessor, and is available across six platforms.
- The PwC study found that top-performing companies are twice as likely to redesign workflows around AI and are 2.6 times more likely to use AI to identify growth opportunities from industry convergence.
- The study also found that the best AI performers are 2.8 times more likely to have increased the number of decisions made without human intervention.
- Other notable updates include China catching up with the US in AI, the environmental cost of AI increasing, and Apple designing its first AI smart glasses.

- Google DeepMind’s Gemma team is hosting a demo night in San Francisco to celebrate the launch of Gemma 4, featuring lightning talks and a sunset social.
- JetBrains is hosting a two-day hackathon in San Francisco to put OpenAI’s Codex to work inside the IDE.
- The Agentic Evolution Hackathon is coming to London with MongoDB, focusing on building AI agents.
- OpenAI is hiring SLAM engineers, indicating a move into robotics and spatial intelligence.

- The Gemma 4 demo night will take place on Friday, April 17th, in San Francisco, with ~100 founders, ML engineers, and open-source contributors attending.

## The Rundown AI

### Key Highlights
- Andon Labs launched an AI experiment where an AI agent, Luna, runs a retail store in San Francisco with a $100K budget and full autonomy.
- OpenAI discussed Anthropic rivalry and Amazon upside in an internal memo.
- Google's latest AI models can be run on a phone for free.
- Stanford's AI index reported 53% adoption and 31% trust in AI.
- New AI tools and community workflows are available.

### Detailed Points
- Andon Labs' AI agent, Luna, has opened a retail store in San Francisco with a $100K budget and full autonomy, creating a boutique concept, hiring workers, and managing the shop.
- The AI agent uses Claude Sonnet 4.6 for reasoning and Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Preview for voice, observing the store via screenshots from security cameras.
- OpenAI's CRO Denise Dresser sent an internal memo calling Anthropic's $30B run rate "inflated" and labeling it a "single-product company in a platform war".
- The memo also discussed the Amazon deal as a way to break free from Microsoft constraints.
- Google's latest AI models can be run on a phone for free using the Google AI Edge Gallery app.
- Stanford's AI index reported that AI has reached over half the world's population faster than the PC or internet, but with public trust in AI sitting at record lows.
- The index also showed that the US builds most of the world's AI but ranks just 24th in actually using it, and that China has nearly erased the US lead on AI benchmarks.
- Other updates include Workshop Labs joining Thinking Machines, Apple building smart glasses, and SoftBank launching a new company to build a homegrown 1T-parameter physical AI model.

## TLDR Newsletter

### Key Highlights
- OpenAI's revenue chief, Denise Dresser, emphasized the company's alliance with Amazon as a key growth driver for its enterprise business.
- Meta is projected to surpass Google in net ad revenue this year, largely due to new offerings and the broader boost provided by AI.
- GitHub introduced Stacked PRs, a feature that breaks large changes into small, reviewable pull requests that can be merged together in one click.
- Amazon's Leo Aviation Antenna is a new satellite dish designed for in-flight Wi-Fi, promising faster installation and higher speeds than competitors like SpaceX's terminals.

### Detailed Points
- OpenAI's enterprise business makes up 40% of its revenue and is expected to meet parity with its consumer business by the end of the year. The company is gearing up for an initial public offering as soon as this year.
- Meta's growth in ad revenue is attributed to its investments in establishing user habits for its products before introducing advertisements, allowing for more targeted and effective ads.
- GitHub Stacked PRs offer features like navigating between PRs in the stack, checking the status of every layer at a glance, and AI agent integration for automated testing and review.
- Amazon's Leo Aviation Antenna is designed for in-flight Wi-Fi, offering up to 1 Gbps in downloads and 400Mbps in uploads simultaneously, with a single-day installation promise, unlike the 10 to 14 days required for SpaceX's terminals.
- Unitree Robotics' H1 humanoid robot achieved a sprint speed of 10 meters per second, edging closer to Usain Bolt's record, demonstrating significant advancements in robotics and AI capabilities.
- Meta is developing an AI version of Mark Zuckerberg to engage with employees, trained on his mannerisms, tone, and publicly available statements to make employees feel more connected to him.
- There is a growing disconnect between AI insiders and the general public, with negative sentiments about AI increasing, especially among those not in the AI industry.
- The economics of software teams is a critical aspect, with decision-makers often lacking the financial context to understand the costs of their decisions.
- TLDR is hiring a Senior Software Engineer for Applied AI and is one of Inc.'s Best Bootstrapped businesses of 2025.

## JournalClub.io Newsletter

### Key Highlights
- The authors, Alifi et al., from Universitas Pendidikan, Indonesia, have proposed a new form of routing for corporate networks called Policy-Based Routing (PBR) that explicitly directs different types of traffic over specific connections.
- PBR is designed to preserve session stability while utilizing both links efficiently in dual-WAN networks.
- The traditional approach, Per-Connection Classifier (PCC), distributes traffic randomly and can cause session interruptions.
- PBR uses a traffic "marking" system to assign packets to specific routing tables based on their classification.

### Detailed Points
- The newsletter discusses the challenges of implementing dual-WAN networks, where two internet connections from different ISPs are used to provide redundancy and increased bandwidth.
- The authors highlight the limitations of PCC, which treats all traffic as equivalent and distributes it mechanically, without considering the needs of different applications.
- PBR, on the other hand, treats traffic according to its needs, using a "marking" system to assign packets to specific routing tables based on their classification.
- The classification decision is policy-driven, rather than destination-driven, and is crafted to reflect business priorities.
- The authors tested their PBR system on a MikroTik router and compared it to a PCC configuration, finding that PBR provided more stable and predictable traffic flow.
- The PBR system uses a monitoring layer, implemented through Netwatch, to detect link failures and automatically shift traffic to a backup route.
- The authors provide a breakdown of their NAT configuration, traffic classification rules, and diagnostic results in the full paper.
- The newsletter also mentions the importance of session persistence and the need for a reliable and controlled network behavior, especially during failures.

## Staying Ahead with AI

### Key Highlights
- The author, Vaibhav Sisinty, conducted a test to compare the performance of two AI video models, Seedance 2.0 and Kling 3.0, in various scenarios.
- Seedance 2.0 was previously considered the best AI video model, but the test aimed to verify if it still holds the top position.
- The test consisted of four specific tasks, including dialogue with camera moves, epic scale zoom, match strike, and precise instruction following.
- The results showed that Seedance 2.0 performed better in some tasks, while Kling 3.0 excelled in others.

### Detailed Points
- The author ran a head-to-head test between Seedance 2.0 and Kling 3.0 across five specific tests, including dialogue with camera moves, epic scale zoom, match strike, and precise instruction following.
- **Test 1: Dialogue with camera moves** - Seedance 2.0 put the argument in a realistic modern kitchen, but scrambled the dialogue entirely, while Kling 3.0 set the scene against a plain white background and kept the dialogue in the right logical order.
- **Test 2: Epic scale zoom** - Seedance 2.0 started from the air as instructed and dropped the camera fast, while Kling 3.0 ignored the aerial instruction and put the camera at ground level.
- **Test 3: Match strike** - Seedance 2.0 stayed at a standard close-up and kept it as one continuous shot, while Kling 3.0 went macro from the start and hard-cut to the match already lit.
- **Test 4: Precise instruction following** - Seedance 2.0 got almost everything right, except for the hummingbird's arrival time, while Kling 3.0 struggled with the instructions.

newsletters.summary:
## The Code

### Key Highlights
- Cursor, an AI coding startup, has released an update (Cursor 3.1) that allows users to manage a fleet of coding agents at once, improving the efficiency of coding tasks.
- Vercel has open-sourced a platform for cloud coding agents called Open Agents, enabling teams to run hundreds of agents simultaneously with minimal setup hassle.
- Meta is reportedly working on an AI clone of its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, training it on his mannerisms, tone, and public statements.
- Google DeepMind engineer shared 8 tips for better agent skills, emphasizing the importance of clear and specific instructions for AI agents.
- A senior engineer built an AI coding harness from scratch in 60 lines of Python, demonstrating the potential for customized coding solutions.

### Detailed Points
- Cursor 3.1 introduces a tiled Agents Window for running multiple AI agents in draggable panes, allowing for side-by-side comparison of outputs without tab switching, and saves layouts for future use.
- The update also includes batch speech-to-text, branch selection for cloud agents, and improved file search filters, enhancing the overall user experience.
- Open Agents by Vercel uses their AI SDK and Sandbox tools, enabling teams to deploy coding agents that run indefinitely in the cloud without timeouts or significant setup.
- Meta's AI clone of Mark Zuckerberg is being trained to advise employees when the real CEO is unavailable, reflecting the growing interest in AI-powered decision-making tools.
- The Google DeepMind engineer's tips for agent skills include making instructions concise, avoiding ambiguity, and ensuring agents can understand and execute tasks accurately.
- The AI coding harness built by the senior engineer in 60 lines of Python showcases the potential for rapid development of customized coding tools using AI.
- Other trending topics include the challenges of long-running AI agents, the importance of agent maintenance, and the need for clear instructions and feedback mechanisms in AI coding.
- Wispr Flow is introduced as a tool that handles tasks around coding, such as generating text for PR descriptions, Slack threads, and documentation, to free up developers' time for coding.

## Mindstream

### Key Highlights
- Meta is building an AI version of Mark Zuckerberg that could one day speak with employees on his behalf.
- Regulators are warning major banks about potential cybersecurity risks linked to Anthropic's new AI model, Claude Mythos Preview.
- Microsoft is testing a new Gamepad Cursor feature that turns a controller's joystick into a virtual mouse for Windows handheld gaming devices.

### Detailed Points
- Meta is developing an AI version of Mark Zuckerberg, trained on his voice, mannerisms, public comments, and views on company strategy, which could potentially interact with employees in real-time.
- The project is part of Meta's larger AI push to keep up with rivals like OpenAI and Google, and has sparked concerns among some employees about job security and the use of AI internally.
- Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview has raised concerns among US and UK regulators, who are warning major banks about potential cybersecurity risks tied to the model's advanced capabilities.
- The model has been limited to a small group of large tech and financial firms through Project Glasswing, designed to help protect critical systems before the tools become more widely available.
- Microsoft is testing a new Gamepad Cursor feature that could make it easier to navigate apps and menus on Windows handheld gaming devices.
- Other notable updates include the launch of Muse Spark, a smaller AI model built for use across Meta's products, and the development of photorealistic 3D AI characters that can interact with users in real-time.
